messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Kwame, a 21-year-old chef working the line at a bustling downtown restaurant, had always prided himself on his precision and control in the kitchen. That control was stolen from him on a humid October night three years ago, after a late shift at his previous job. He had walked out the back door into the alley, still smelling of garlic and grill smoke, when a man he vaguely recognized from the neighbourhood cornered him. The assault was fast, brutal, and silent except for the sound of a car door slamming somewhere down the block and the low rumble of an idling engine that never drove away. Kwame remembered the weight of the man’s forearm across his throat, the concrete scraping his spine, and a sickening certainty that he could not move, could not speak, could not stop what was happening. When it was over, the engine revved once and then faded into the night.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame did not tell anyone. He showered for hours, scrubbing his skin raw, and began checking his body every morning for bruises or scratches he might have missed—a habit that soon became a compulsion he performed half a dozen times a day, even in the walk-in cooler at work, where he would press his back against the metal shelves and run his hands over his ribs and hips, searching for evidence of injury. The memory of the assault did not so much return as ambush him. A car backfiring outside the restaurant’s delivery bay would drop him onto the floor of that alley before he could register what was happening; he would hear the engine sound in his head again, so vivid and real that he would glance around the kitchen to see if anyone else could hear it. When a line cook once grabbed his shoulder from behind to reach past him for a pan, Kwame spun around with a chef’s knife still in his hand, his heart hammering, certain for a split second that the alley was back and his body was pinned again. The cook laughed it off, but Kwame saw the flicker of unease in his eyes.

Other triggers proved just as destabilizing. One night during a crowded Friday service, a prep cook slammed a metal pan onto the counter in frustration; the sharp, violent sound sent Kwame’s mind reeling not to the alley but to a strange, dissociated place where he saw himself on that concrete floor from above, a distant figure who could not move, and for a moment he was not sure whether the man on the ground was really him. The sensation passed in seconds, but it left him cold and confused—what kind of memory was it if he did not fully feel like it was his own? On another occasion, the head chef gave him a sudden, rapid-fire series of orders during a rush, and Kwame’s station fell into chaos. As the tickets piled up and he lost the rhythm, the feeling of helplessness—of having no control over what was happening to his body—flooded back. He froze mid-motion, spatula in hand, unable to move his arms, and the dishwasher had to shake him out of it. That night, Kwame went home and sat in the dark, terrified of how easily loss of control—any loss of control—could pull him back into that alley.

He tried to explain to a colleague later what had happened, but the words came out in fragments—“the door, the car, I couldn’t…”—and he gave up, feeling stupid and exposed. After that, he stopped trying to talk about it altogether. Instead, he found himself rehearsing other outcomes in his head: what he should have done, what he would do if he ever saw that man again. The revenge fantasies became a private ritual, detailed and satisfying, but they left him feeling hollow and ashamed because they confirmed what he already believed—that he had acted in ways that went against who he was. A real man, he told himself, would have fought back, would have stopped it. Somebody else would have known how to get away. Somebody else would not have frozen.

At home, a small studio apartment above a laundromat, Kwame could not let his guard down. He slept with the lights on and a chef’s knife under his pillow. Every creak from the floorboards made him alert, every sudden movement from a neighbour’s shadow past his blinds sent him to the door to check the lock twice. He had stopped dating entirely, convinced that intimacy would only lead to another moment of helplessness, and he had begun to think of his future as a flat wall: he could not imagine advancing in his career, could not picture a partner, could not see himself surviving five more years of this watchfulness.

Three weeks ago, a delivery truck backfired directly outside the restaurant’s open back door while Kwame was plating a busy Saturday night dinner. He dropped a tray of entrees, dove behind the counter, and came up swinging a spatula at a dishwasher who had simply reached for a rag. The head chef sent him home early, concerned but confused. That night, alone in his apartment, Kwame sat on the edge of his bed and realised he could not keep living inside this loop of hypervigilance and rage. He wanted to stop checking his body, stop bracing for the sound of an engine, stop believing that his future had already ended in an alley. He wanted, more than anything, to be able to explain what had happened to him without losing the thread. He called a clinic the next morning and scheduled an intake, terrified that even now, sitting in a waiting room, he would not be able to finish the story.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Demographics: trauma_type (Sexual assault): The vignette describes a general assault in an alley but does not specify that it was sexual assault, which is the patient's reported trauma type.
- Self-report: Triggers - Violence: The vignette does not depict the patient being triggered by witnessing or encountering violence separate from the original assault. The triggers shown are car sounds, sudden movements, and loss of control, but not explicitly violence.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Kwame, a 21-year-old chef working the line at a bustling downtown restaurant, had always prided himself on his precision and control in the kitchen. That control was stolen from him on a humid October night three years ago, after a late shift at his previous job. He had walked out the back door into the alley, still smelling of garlic and grill smoke, when a man he vaguely recognized from the neighbourhood cornered him. The assault was fast, brutal, and sexual—Kwame remembered the weight of the man’s forearm across his throat, the concrete scraping his spine, the sickening violation as the man forced himself inside him, and a certain, drowning terror that he could not move, could not speak, could not stop what was happening. When it was over, the man zipped his pants and walked away; a car engine revved somewhere down the block and then faded into the night, leaving Kwame alone on the cold ground.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame did not tell anyone. He showered for hours, scrubbing his skin raw, and began checking his body every morning for bruises or scratches he might have missed—a habit that soon became a compulsion he performed half a dozen times a day, even in the walk-in cooler at work, where he would press his back against the metal shelves and run his hands over his ribs, his hips, his inner thighs, searching for evidence of injury he already knew was not there. The memory of the assault did not so much return as ambush him. A car backfiring outside the restaurant’s delivery bay would drop him onto the floor of that alley before he could register what was happening; he would hear the engine sound in his head again, so vivid and real that he would glance around the kitchen to see if anyone else could hear it. When a line cook once grabbed his shoulder from behind to reach past him for a pan, Kwame spun around with a chef’s knife still in his hand, his heart hammering, certain for a split second that the alley was back and his body was pinned again. The cook laughed it off, but Kwame saw the flicker of unease in his eyes.

Other triggers proved just as destabilizing. One night during a crowded Friday service, a prep cook slammed a metal pan onto the counter in frustration; the sharp, violent sound sent Kwame’s mind reeling not to the alley but to a strange, dissociated place where he saw himself on that concrete floor from above, a distant figure who could not move, and for a moment he was not sure whether the man on the ground was really him. The sensation passed in seconds, but it left him cold and confused—what kind of memory was it if he did not fully feel like it was his own? On another occasion, the head chef gave him a sudden, rapid-fire series of orders during a rush, and Kwame’s station fell into chaos. As the tickets piled up and he lost the rhythm, the feeling of helplessness—of having no control over what was happening to his body—flooded back. He froze mid-motion, spatula in hand, unable to move his arms, and the dishwasher had to shake him out of it. That night, Kwame went home and sat in the dark, terrified of how easily loss of control—any loss of control—could pull him back into that alley.

The most unexpected trigger came one afternoon when Kwame was walking to the bus stop and saw two teenagers shoving each other outside a convenience store. One boy grabbed the other by the collar and shoved him against a wall; the sound of the impact—a hollow thud of body on brick—hit Kwame like a physical blow. His chest tightened, his vision blurred, and for a horrifying moment he was back in the alley, the man’s weight on him, the scrape of concrete against his spine. He stumbled into a doorway, breathing fast, and had to call in sick to work because he could not stop shaking. After that, he began to avoid the neighbourhood around the convenience store, taking a longer route home even when it made him late. He tried to explain to a colleague later what had happened, but the words came out in fragments—“the door, the car, I couldn’t…”—and he gave up, feeling stupid and exposed. After that, he stopped trying to talk about it altogether. Instead, he found himself rehearsing other outcomes in his head: what he should have done, what he would do if he ever saw that man again. The revenge fantasies became a private ritual, detailed and satisfying, but they left him feeling hollow and ashamed because they confirmed what he already believed—that he had acted in ways that went against who he was. A real man, he told himself, would have fought back, would have stopped it from happening, would have known how to get away. Somebody else would not have frozen.

At home, a small studio apartment above a laundromat, Kwame could not let his guard down. He slept with the lights on and a chef’s knife under his pillow. Every creak from the floorboards made him alert, every sudden movement from a neighbour’s shadow past his blinds sent him to the door to check the lock twice. He had stopped dating entirely, convinced that intimacy would only lead to another moment of helplessness, and he had begun to think of his future as a flat wall: he could not imagine advancing in his career, could not picture a partner, could not see himself surviving five more years of this watchfulness.

Three weeks ago, a delivery truck backfired directly outside the restaurant’s open back door while Kwame was plating a busy Saturday night dinner. He dropped a tray of entrees, dove behind the counter, and came up swinging a spatula at a dishwasher who had simply reached for a rag. The head chef sent him home early, concerned but confused. That night, alone in his apartment, Kwame sat on the edge of his bed and realised he could not keep living inside this loop of hypervigilance and rage. He wanted to stop checking his body, stop bracing for the sound of an engine, stop flinching at the sight of a shoving match on the street, stop believing that his future had already ended in an alley. He wanted, more than anything, to be able to explain what had happened to him without losing the thread. He called a clinic the next morning and scheduled an intake, terrified that even now, sitting in a waiting room, he would not be able to finish the story.
